outputs.L1: **Method for Visualizing a Tooth Situation.** The invention relates to a method for visualizing a tooth situation. An image of a patient’s face is captured and stored as a facial data record (1). Feature points (3) within the facial data record (1) are automatically identified using a facial recognition method. Based on these feature points (3), a mouth area (4) located between the lips is automatically identified, along with the position of the face and a three-dimensional direction (5) representing the orientation of the face within the facial data record (1). A virtual tooth data record (2) of the tooth situation is oriented in accordance with the three-dimensional direction (5) of the face and positioned relative to the facial data record (1) according to the position of the face. The mouth area within the facial data record (1) is then partially overlaid, overlaid, and/or replaced by the tooth data record (2), and the result is displayed as a visualization data record.
outputs.L2: **Method for displaying a dental condition.** The invention concerns a technique for depicting a patient’s dental condition. An image of the patient’s face is captured and saved as a facial dataset (1). A facial-recognition process automatically identifies feature points (3) in that dataset. Using these points, the system automatically detects the mouth region (4) between the lips and determines both the face’s position within the facial dataset (1) and the three-dimensional direction (5) in which the face is oriented. A virtual dental dataset (2) representing the dental condition is then aligned with the face’s three-dimensional orientation and placed relative to its detected position in the facial dataset (1). The dental dataset (2) partially covers, fully covers, and/or replaces the mouth region in the facial dataset, and the resulting composite is presented as a visualization dataset.
outputs.L3:
An image of the patient’s face is first captured and stored as a facial data record. Facial-recognition technology then analyzes the image to identify relevant facial feature points and delineate the mouth area between the lips. Based on these feature points, the system determines the position of the patient’s face and its three-dimensional orientation.

A virtual tooth data record is subsequently aligned with the detected facial position and orientation to ensure anatomically appropriate placement. The virtual teeth are then superimposed over, or used to replace, part or all of the identified mouth area. The resulting composite image is generated and displayed as a visualization data record, providing a preview of the patient’s face with the virtual dental configuration.
outputs.L4:
The method provides a realistic visualization of a patient’s current or proposed dental situation by combining facial-image analysis with a virtual tooth model. First, one or more images of the patient’s face are captured using a camera or obtained from an existing image source. A facial-recognition or image-processing system analyzes the image to identify characteristic facial landmarks, such as the eyes, nose, lips, corners of the mouth, and facial contour. Based on these landmarks, the system determines the location and dimensions of the mouth area and estimates the position, scale, and three-dimensional orientation of the patient’s face relative to the camera.

A virtual tooth dataset is then selected or generated. The dataset may represent the patient’s existing teeth, a planned dental restoration, or a simulated treatment result. Using the detected landmarks and the estimated facial pose, the system scales, rotates, translates, and, where appropriate, deforms the virtual tooth model so that it corresponds to the patient’s mouth and facial orientation. Additional adjustments may be made to account for perspective, lip position, tooth visibility, lighting, color, and partial obstruction by the lips or surrounding facial tissue.

After alignment, the virtual teeth are incorporated into the facial image. In one implementation, the tooth model is superimposed on the visible mouth region. In another, all or part of the original mouth or tooth area is replaced with a rendered view of the virtual dental dataset. Image blending, masking, shading, and color correction may be applied to create a natural transition between the virtual teeth and the surrounding face.

The resulting composite image presents a realistic visualization of the patient’s dental condition or anticipated treatment outcome in the context of the patient’s own face. This visualization can assist with diagnosis, treatment planning, communication between dental professionals, and presentation of possible cosmetic or restorative results to the patient.

## The Method

A method is more than a set of instructions. It is an organized way of turning an idea into action and a problem into a solution. Whether used in science, education, business, or everyday life, a good method provides structure, consistency, and direction.

The first step in any effective method is to define the goal clearly. Once the desired outcome is understood, the process can be divided into manageable stages. Each stage should have a purpose, and its results should be evaluated before moving forward. This makes it easier to identify mistakes, improve efficiency, and adapt to unexpected circumstances.

However, no method should be treated as permanent or inflexible. Conditions change, new information becomes available, and different situations may require different approaches. The most useful method is therefore one that combines clear principles with room for adjustment.

Ultimately, the method matters because it shapes the result. A thoughtful process does not guarantee success, but it increases the likelihood of achieving reliable, repeatable, and meaningful outcomes.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract for an invention that detects facial landmarks and the mouth area in a patient photo, aligns a 3D tooth dataset with the face, and displays the resulting visualization.
counterfactuals.output: A computer-implemented system and method are disclosed for visualizing a three-dimensional tooth dataset in relation to a patient’s face. A processor receives a patient facial image and detects facial landmarks, including landmarks defining a mouth region. The processor determines facial orientation and spatial characteristics of the mouth region from the detected landmarks, and transforms a three-dimensional tooth dataset by translation, rotation, and scaling to align the dataset with the patient’s face and mouth. The aligned tooth dataset is rendered with the facial image to generate a composite visualization in which virtual teeth are positioned relative to the detected mouth region. The visualization may be displayed through a user interface that permits adjustment of the alignment, viewing perspective, tooth configuration, or rendering properties. The disclosed techniques facilitate consistent, automated presentation of tooth geometry in a facial context for treatment planning, simulation, and patient communication.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a method for creating a virtual dental preview by analyzing a facial image, determining the face’s position and orientation, and overlaying a digital tooth model onto the mouth.
counterfactuals.output:
A virtual dental preview can be created with the following image-processing pipeline:

1. **Acquire and preprocess the facial image**
   - Capture a frontal or oblique facial photograph.
   - Correct lens distortion, normalize lighting and color, and crop the face region.
   - If available, use camera calibration data or a known-size reference for scale.

2. **Detect facial and oral landmarks**
   - Apply a facial-landmark model to locate the eyes, nose, jaw, and lip contours.
   - Detect mouth-specific features such as the lip corners, upper and lower lip boundaries, dental midline, and any visible teeth.

3. **Estimate face position and orientation**
   - Fit the detected landmarks to a generic 3D face model.
   - Use a perspective-n-point or similar pose-estimation algorithm to determine head translation and yaw, pitch, and roll.
   - Estimate the mouth plane, dental arch direction, and image scale from the fitted model.

4. **Prepare the digital tooth model**
   - Select or generate a 2D or 3D model representing the proposed tooth arrangement.
   - Adjust tooth dimensions, spacing, curvature, color, and gingival outline using clinical measurements or treatment parameters.

5. **Register the tooth model to the mouth**
   - Establish correspondences between model landmarks—such as the dental midline, incisal edge, and arch endpoints—and the detected oral landmarks.
   - Compute a rigid, affine, projective, or 3D perspective transformation that aligns the tooth model with the estimated mouth position and head pose.
   - Optionally deform the model to follow the patient’s smile arc and lip curvature.

6. **Handle visibility and occlusion**
   - Create masks for the upper lip, lower lip, cheeks, and existing intraoral region.
   - Render only the portions of the digital teeth that would be visible through the mouth opening.
   - Use depth ordering so the lips naturally cover the tooth model.

7. **Render and blend**
   - Render the transformed tooth model using lighting consistent with the photograph.
   - Match brightness, color temperature, shadows, sharpness, and image noise.
   - Feather mask boundaries and add subtle reflections or translucency to produce a realistic composite.

8. **Provide interactive refinement**
   - Allow the user or clinician to adjust model position, rotation, scale, tooth shape, shade, and smile width.
   - Recalculate the overlay in real time and export the resulting preview.

For improved accuracy, multiple photographs, depth-camera data, or a dental scan can be registered to the facial image. The result should be presented as a visualization rather than a guaranteed prediction of treatment outcome.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise technical explanation of how facial feature points can be used to position and orient a virtual tooth dataset within an image of a patient’s face.
counterfactuals.output:
Facial feature points provide anatomical references for registering a virtual tooth model to a patient image:

1. **Detect landmarks:** Identify points such as the pupils, nose tip, facial midline, lip corners, and visible dental landmarks.
2. **Define a facial coordinate frame:** The interpupillary line estimates horizontal orientation, while the nose–philtrum–chin axis defines the facial midline. Distances between landmarks provide image scale.
3. **Estimate tooth position:** Lip corners and the mouth opening constrain the dental arch’s center, width, and vertical placement.
4. **Estimate orientation:** Align the virtual dental midline with the facial midline and the occlusal plane with an appropriate horizontal reference, often the interpupillary or commissure line.
5. **Register and project:** Compute a 2D similarity/affine transform for simple overlays, or estimate a 3D rigid pose and camera projection when using a 3D tooth dataset. Optimize the transform by minimizing landmark reprojection error.
6. **Apply masking:** Use lip and facial contours as occlusion masks so teeth appear correctly behind the lips.

The result is a scaled, translated, and rotated tooth dataset anatomically aligned with the patient’s face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an invention summary titled “Method for visualizing a tooth situation,” preserving reference numerals for the facial data record, tooth data record, feature points, mouth area, and face orientation.
counterfactuals.output:
# Method for Visualizing a Tooth Situation

The invention relates to a computer-implemented method for visualizing a tooth situation of a person. A facial data record **(1)** representing at least part of the person’s face is acquired, and a tooth data record **(2)** representing at least part of the person’s dentition is provided. Feature points **(3)** are identified in the facial data record **(1)** and used to determine a mouth area **(4)** and a face orientation **(5)**.

The tooth data record **(2)** is spatially aligned with the facial data record **(1)** based on the feature points **(3)**, the mouth area **(4)**, and/or the face orientation **(5)**. A combined visualization is then generated in which the tooth situation represented by the tooth data record **(2)** is displayed in a position and orientation corresponding to the person’s face. The method enables a realistic visualization of an existing, planned, or simulated tooth situation and may be used for dental diagnosis, treatment planning, or presentation of an anticipated treatment result.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
